c: Joshua

Joshua, son of Nun, was Moses’ assistant and successor as Israel’s leader. Joshua brought the young nation across the Jordan River into the Promised Land of Canaan, faithfully following God’s leadership.
Before Israel reached Mount Sinai, Joshua led Israel’s warriors when Amalek attacked Israel (
). Shortly thereafter, he was among the twelve men Moses sent to scout the Promised Land (
). Against popular opinion, Joshua and Caleb urged Israel to occupy Canaan immediately (
), and as a result, of the twelve spies, only they entered Canaan (
God directed Moses to designate Joshua as his successor (
). After Moses died, Joshua led Israel across the Jordan River (
) to the conquest of Jericho (
). When Israel suffered defeat at Ai, Joshua turned to the Lord and followed his instructions to purge Israel of sin (
); then Israel conquered Ai (
). Following God’s instructions to Moses (
), Joshua built an altar on Mount Ebal (
) and read the blessings and curses of the covenant (
). Joshua conducted campaigns against two coalitions of Canaanite kings, a southern and a northern coalition (
). Joshua’s victories in these campaigns opened the hill country to settlement by the Israelites.
After supervising the allotment of territories to the tribes of Israel, Joshua received his own portion in the land of Ephraim (
). He established the cities of refuge (
) and the Levitical cities (ch
) and released the 2½ tribes that had settled east of the Jordan River to return home (
). As he grew old, Joshua charged Israel to remain faithful to God (

). His farewell message at Shechem summarized God’s dealings with Israel and concluded with the familiar challenge, “Choose today whom you will serve. . . . But as for me and my family, we will serve the
Lord
). Joshua died at the age of 110 and was buried in Timnath-serah (
Joshua demonstrated exceptional faithfulness throughout his life, except in dealing with the Gibeonites (
), when he neglected to consult the Lord regarding a decision. Israel served God faithfully under Joshua and the elders Joshua trained (
). Stephen mentions Joshua in his martyr’s sermon (
), and the writer of Hebrews uses Joshua’s conquest of Jericho as an illustration of faith (
). It is fitting that Joshua and Jesus are the same name in Hebrew: Joshua led Israel into physical salvation in Canaan; Jesus leads all who believe in him into eternal salvation.

This second major section of the book includes a record of Joshua’s southern and northern campaigns against two coalitions of Canaanite kings. Joshua’s victories enabled Israel to settle the hill country from Galilee in the north to the Negev in the south.

Joshua and the Israelite armies

faithfully carried out the tasks God gave them. This summary showcases their successes, providing proper recognition for their faithfulness. God gave the Israelites their promised inheritance while bringing about the long-delayed judgment of the Canaanites. This roster of defeated kings, identified by their city-states, provides evidence of God’s accomplished purposes. A solemn yet joyful recital for Israel, the list symbolizes God’s mighty acts for his people and exalts his own great name.
Baal-gad
was at the western foot of Mount Hermon, the northern limit of Joshua’s conquests west of the Jordan. •
The valley of Lebanon
divided the coastal Lebanon range and the inland Anti-Lebanon range. •
Mount Halak, which leads up to Seir
(i.e., Edom), marked the southern limit of Joshua’s conquests.
